entries.5cdd5075cfae96340b65c795059213ce82522bff: <div sID="gen10938" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="33" osisID="Ps.33" sID="Ps.33"/> <div eID="gen10938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10939" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10940" type="x-p"/> This is a psalm of praise; it is probable that David was the penman of it, but we are not told so, because God would have us look above the penmen of sacred writ, to that blessed Spirit that moved and guided them. The psalmist, in this psalm, I. Calls upon the righteous to praise God, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.1-Ps.33.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Furnishes us with matter for praise. We must praise God, 1. For his justice, goodness, and truth, appearing in his word, and in all his works, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.4-Ps.33.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. 2. For his power appearing in the work of creation, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.6-Ps.33.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. 3. For the sovereignty of his providence in the government of the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.10-Ps.33.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>) and again, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.13-Ps.33.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. 4. For the peculiar favour which he bears to his own chosen people, which encourages them to trust in him (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.12">ver. 12</reference>) and again, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.18-Ps.33.22">ver. 18-22</reference>. We need not be at a loss for proper thoughts in singing this psalm, which so naturally expresses the pious affections of a devout soul towards God.
entries.ad205ec95c2223d01cbb8894ecddf7ac73a1ff59: <div eID="gen10940" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10939" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">An Exhortation to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen10941" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Rejoice in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , O ye righteous: <hi type="italic">for</hi> praise is comely for the upright. <hi type="super">2</hi> Praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery <hi type="italic">and</hi> an instrument of ten strings. <hi type="super">3</hi> Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> right; and all his works <hi type="italic">are done</hi> in truth. <hi type="super">5</hi> He loveth righteousness and judgment: the earth is full of the goodness of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> By the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth. <hi type="super">7</hi> He gathereth the waters of the sea together as a heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses. <hi type="super">8</hi> Let all the earth fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him. <hi type="super">9</hi> For he spake, and it was <hi type="italic">done;</hi> he commanded, and it stood fast. <hi type="super">10</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect. <hi type="super">11</hi> The counsel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations. <div eID="gen10941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10942" type="x-p"/> Four things the psalmist expresses in these verses: <div eID="gen10942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10943" type="x-p"/> I. The great desire he had that God might be praised. He did not think he did it so well himself, but that he wished others also might be employed in this work; the more the better, in this concert: it is the more like heaven. 1. Holy joy is the heart and soul of praise, and that is here pressed upon all good people (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous;</hi> so the foregoing psalm concluded and so this begins; for all our religious exercises should both begin and end with a holy complacency and triumph in God as the best of being and best of friends. 2. Thankful praise is the breath and language of holy joy; and that also is here required of us (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Praise the Lord;</hi> speak well of him, and give him the glory due to his name." 3. Religious songs are the proper expressions of thankful praise; those are here required (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Sing unto him a new song,</hi> the best you have, not that which by frequent use is worn, thread-bare, but that which, being new, is most likely to move the affections, a new song for new mercies and upon every new occasion, for those compassions which are new every morning." Music was then used, by the appointment of David, with the temple-songs, that they might be the better sung; and this also is here called for (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sing unto him with the psaltery.</hi> Here is, (1.) A good rule for this duty: "Do it <hi type="italic">skilfully,</hi> and <hi type="italic">with a loud noise;</hi> let it have the best both of head and heart; let it be done intelligently and with a clear head, affectionately and with a warm heart." (2.) A good reason for this duty: <hi type="italic">For praise is comely for the upright.</hi> It is well pleasing to God (the garments of praise add much to the comeliness which God puts upon his people) and it is an excellent ornament to our profession. <hi type="italic">It becomes the upright,</hi> whom God has put so much honour upon, to give honour to him. The upright praise God in a comely manner, for they praise him with their hearts, that is praising him with their glory; whereas the praises of hypocrites are awkward and uncomely, like <hi type="italic">a parable in the mouth of fools,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.7">Prov. xxvi. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen10943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10944" type="x-p"/> II. The high thoughts he had of God, and of his infinite perfections, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.4-Ps.33.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. God makes himself known to us, 1. In his <hi type="italic">word,</hi> here put for all divine revelation, all that which God at sundry times and in divers manners spoke to the children of men, and that is all <hi type="italic">right,</hi> there is nothing amiss in it; his commands exactly agree with the rules of equity and the eternal reasons of good and evil. His promises are all wise and good and inviolably sure, and there is no iniquity in his threatenings, but even those are designed for our good, by deterring us from evil. God's word is right, and therefore all our deviations from it are wrong, and we are then in the right when we agree with it. 2. In his <hi type="italic">works,</hi> and those are all <hi type="italic">done in truth,</hi> all according to his counsels, which are called the <hi type="italic">scriptures of truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Dan. x. 21</reference>. The copy in all God's works agrees exactly with the great original, the plan laid in the Eternal Mind, and varies not in the least jot. God has made it to appear in his works, (1.) That he is a God of inflexible justice: <hi type="italic">He loveth righteousness and judgment.</hi> There is nothing but righteousness in the sentence he passes and judgment in the execution of it. He never did nor can do wrong to any of his creatures, but is always ready to give redress to those that are wronged, and does it with delight. He takes pleasure in those that are righteous. He is himself the righteous Lord, and therefore loveth righteousness. (2.) That he is a God of inexhaustible bounty: <hi type="italic">The earth is full of his goodness,</hi> that is, of the proofs and instances of it. The benign influences which the earth receives from above, and the fruits it is thereby enabled to produce, the provision that is made both for man and beast, and the common blessings with which all the nations of the earth are blessed, plainly declare that <hi type="italic">the earth is full of his goodness</hi>—the darkest, the coldest, the hottest, and the most dry and desert part of it not excepted. What a pity is it that this earth, which is so full of God's goodness, should be so empty of his praises, and that of the multitudes that live upon his bounty there are so few that live to his glory! <div eID="gen10944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10945" type="x-p"/> III. The conviction he was under of the almighty power of God, evidenced in the creation of the world. We "believe in God," and therefore we praise him as "the Father Almighty, maker of heaven and earth," so we are here taught to praise him. Observe, <div eID="gen10945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10946" type="x-p"/> 1. How God made the world, and brought all things into being. (1.) How easily: All things were made <hi type="italic">by the word of the Lord and by the breath of his mouth.</hi> Christ is the Word, the Spirit is the breath, so that God the Father made the world, as he rules it and redeems it, by his Son and Spirit. <hi type="italic">He spoke, and he commanded</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.9">v. 9</reference>), and that was enough; there needed no more. With men saying and doing are two things, but it is not so with God. By the Word and Spirit of God as the world was made, so was man, that little world. God said, <hi type="italic">Let us make man,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">breathed into him the breath of life.</hi> By the Word and Spirit the church is built, that new world, and grace wrought in the soul, that new man, that new creation. What cannot that power do which with a word made a world! (2.) How effectually it was done: <hi type="italic">And it stood fast.</hi> What God does he does to purpose; he does it and it stands fast. <hi type="italic">Whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>. It is by virtue of that command to stand fast that things <hi type="italic">continue to this day according to God's ordinance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.91">Ps. cxix. 91</reference>. <div eID="gen10946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10947" type="x-p"/> 2. What he made. He made all things, but notice is here taken, (1.) of <hi type="italic">the heavens, and the host of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.33.6">v. 6</reference>. The visible heavens, and the sun, moon, and stars, their hosts—(2.) Of the waters, and the treasures of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.7">v. 7</reference>. The earth was at first covered with the water, and, being heavier, must of course subside and sink under it; but, to show from the very first that the God of nature is not tied to the ordinary method of nature, and the usual operations of his powers, with a word's speaking <hi type="italic">he gathered the waters together on a heap,</hi> that the dry land might appear, yet left them not to continue on a heap, but <hi type="italic">laid up the depth in store-houses,</hi> not only in the flats where the seas make their beds, and in which they are locked up by the sand on the shore as in storehouses, but in secret subterraneous caverns, where they are hidden from the eyes of all living, but were reserved as in a store-house for that day when those fountains of the great deep were to be broken up; and they are still laid up there in store, for which use the great Master of the house knows best. <div eID="gen10947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10948" type="x-p"/> 3. What use is to be made of this (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let all the earth fear the Lord,</hi> and <hi type="italic">stand in awe of him;</hi> that is, let all the children of men worship him and give glory to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.5-Ps.95.6">Ps. xc. 5, 6</reference>. The everlasting gospel gives this as the reason why we must worship God, because he made the heaven, and the earth, and the sea, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 6, 7</reference>. Let us all fear him, that is, dread his wrath and displeasure, and be afraid of having him our enemy and of standing it out against him. Let us not dare to offend him who having this power no doubt has all power in his hand. It is dangerous being at war with him who has the host of heaven for his armies and the depths of the sea for his magazines, and therefore it is wisdom to desire conditions of peace, see <reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer. v. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen10948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10949" type="x-p"/> IV. The satisfaction he had of God's sovereignty and dominion, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.10-Ps.33.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. He over-rules all the counsels of men, and makes them, contrary to their intention, serviceable to his counsels. Come and see with an eye of faith God in the throne, 1. Frustrating the devices of his enemies: <hi type="italic">He bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought,</hi> so that what they imagine against him and his kingdom proves <hi type="italic">a vain thing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>); the counsel of Ahithophel is turned into foolishness; Haman's plot is baffled. Though the design be laid ever so deep, and the hopes raised upon it ever so high, yet, if God says it <hi type="italic">shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass;</hi> it is all to no purpose. 2. Fulfilling his own decrees: <hi type="italic">The counsel of the Lord standeth for ever.</hi> It is immutable in itself, <hi type="italic">for he is in one mind, and who can turn him?</hi> The execution of it may be opposed, but cannot in the least be obstructed by any created power. Through all the revolutions of time God never changed his measures, but in every event, even that which to us is most surprising, the eternal counsel of God is fulfilled, nor can any thing prevent its being accomplished in its time. With what pleasure to ourselves may we in singing this give praise to God! How easy may this thought make us at all times, that God governs the world, that he did it in infinite wisdom before we were born, and will do it when we are silent in the dust!
entries.f6ba15648efd79218ccdf09a7ea09eafe09d85d5: <div eID="gen10949" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Sovereign Power.</title> <div sID="gen10950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the nation whose God <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="italic">and</hi> the people <hi type="italic">whom</hi> he hath chosen for his own inheritance. <hi type="super">13</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> looketh from heaven; he beholdeth all the sons of men. <hi type="super">14</hi> From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth. <hi type="super">15</hi> He fashioneth their hearts alike; he considereth all their works. <hi type="super">16</hi> There is no king saved by the multitude of a host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength. <hi type="super">17</hi> A horse <hi type="italic">is</hi> a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver <hi type="italic">any</hi> by his great strength. <hi type="super">18</hi> Behold, the eye of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy; <hi type="super">19</hi> To deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine. <hi type="super">20</hi> Our soul waiteth for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : he <hi type="italic">is</hi> our help and our shield. <hi type="super">21</hi> For our heart shall rejoice in him, because we have trusted in his holy name. <hi type="super">22</hi> Let thy mercy, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , be upon us, according as we hope in thee. <div eID="gen10950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10951" type="x-p"/> We are here taught to give to God the glory, <div eID="gen10951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10952" type="x-p"/> I. Of his common providence towards all the children of men. Though he has endued man with understanding and freedom of will, yet he reserves to himself the government of him, and even of those very faculties by which he is qualified to govern himself. 1. The children of men are all under his eye, even their hearts are so; and all the motions and operations of their souls, which none know but they themselves, he knows better than they themselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.13-Ps.33.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Though the residence of God's glory is in the highest heavens, yet thence he not only has a prospect of all the earth, but a particular inspection of all the inhabitants of the earth. He not only beholds them, but he <hi type="italic">looks upon them;</hi> he looks narrowly upon them (so the word here used is sometimes rendered), so narrowly that not the least thought can escape his observation. Atheists think that, because he dwells above in heaven, he cannot, or will not, take notice of what is done here in this lower world; but thence, high as it is, he sees us all, and all persons and things are naked and open before him. 2. Their hearts, as well as their times, are all in his hand: <hi type="italic">He fashions their hearts.</hi> He made them at first, formed the spirit of each man within him, then when he brought him into being. Hence he is called <hi type="italic">the Father of spirits:</hi> and this is a good argument to prove that he perfectly knows them. The artist that made the clock, can account for the motions of every wheel. David uses this argument with application to himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Ps. cxxxix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">14</reference>. He still moulds the hearts of men, turns them as the rivers of water, which way soever he pleases, to serve his own purposes, darkens or enlightens men's understandings, stiffens or bows their wills, according as he is pleased to make use of them. He that fashions men's hearts fashions them alike. It is in hearts as in faces, though there is a great difference, and such a variety as that no two faces are exactly of the same features, nor any two hearts exactly of the same temper, yet there is such a similitude that, in some things, all faces and all hearts agree, <hi type="italic">as in water face answers to face,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.19">Prov. xxvii. 19</reference>. He <hi type="italic">fashions them together</hi> (so some read it); as the wheels of a watch, though of different shapes, sizes, and motions, are yet all put together, to serve one and the same purpose, so the hearts of men and their dispositions, however varying from each other and seeming to contradict one another, are yet all overruled to serve the divine purpose, which is one. 3. They, and all they do, are obnoxious to his judgment; <hi type="italic">for he considers all their works,</hi> not only knows them, but weighs them, that he may render to every man according to his works, in the day, in the world, of retribution, in the judgment, and to eternity. 4. All the powers of the creature have a dependence upon him, and are of no account, of no avail at all, without him, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.16-Ps.33.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. It is much for the honour of God that not only no force can prevail in opposition to him, but that no force can act but in dependence on him and by a power derived from him. (1.) The strength of a king is nothing without God. No king is sacred by his royal prerogatives, or the authority with which he is invested; for the powers that are, of that kind, are ordained of God, and are what he makes them, and no more. David was a king, and a man of war from his youth, and yet acknowledged God to be his only protector and Saviour. (2.) The strength of an army is nothing without God. <hi type="italic">The multitude of a host</hi> cannot secure those under whose command they act, unless God make them a security to them. A great army cannot be sure of victory; for, when God pleases, one shall chase a thousand. (3.) The strength of a giant is nothing without God. <hi type="italic">A mighty man,</hi> such as Goliath was, <hi type="italic">is not delivered by</hi> his <hi type="italic">much strength,</hi> when his day comes to fall. Neither the firmness and activity of his body nor the stoutness and resolution of his mind will stand him in any stead, any further than God is pleased to give him success. <hi type="italic">Let not the strong man</hi> then <hi type="italic">glory in his strength,</hi> but let us all strengthen ourselves in the Lord our God, go forth, and go on, in his strength. (4.) The strength of a horse is nothing without God (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">A horse is a vain thing for safety.</hi> In war horses were then so highly accounted of, and so much depended on, that God forbade the kings of Israel to <hi type="italic">multiply horses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">Deut. xvii. 16</reference>), lest they should be tempted to trust to them and their confidence should thereby be taken off from God. David houghed the horses of the Syrians (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. viii. 4</reference>); here he houghs all the horses in the world, by pronouncing a horse a vain thing for safety in the day of battle. If the war-horse be unruly and ill-managed, he may hurry his rider into danger instead of carrying him out of danger. If he be killed under him, he may be his death, instead of saving his life. It is therefore our interest to make sure God's favour towards us, and then we may be sure of his power engaged for us, and need not fear whatever is against us. <div eID="gen10952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10953" type="x-p"/> II. We are to give God the glory of his special grace. In the midst of his acknowledgments of God's providence he pronounces those blessed that have Jehovah for their God, who governs the world, and has wherewithal to help them in every time of need, while those were miserable who had this and the other Baal for their god, which was so far from being able to hear and help them that is was itself senseless and helpless (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord,</hi> even Israel, who had the knowledge of the true God and were taken into covenant with him, and all others who own God for theirs and are owned by him; for they also, whatever nation they are of, are of the spiritual seed of Abraham. 1. It is their wisdom that they take the Lord for their God, that they direct their homage and adoration there where it is due and where the payment of it will not be in vain. 2. It is their happiness that they are the people whom God has chosen for his own inheritance, whom he is pleased with, and honoured in, and whom he protects and takes care of, whom he cultivates and improves as a man does his inheritance, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.9">Deut. xxxii. 9</reference>. Now let us observe here, to the honour of divine grace, (1.) The regard which God has to his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.18-Ps.33.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. God beholds all the sons of men with an eye of observation, but his eye of favour and complacency is upon those that fear him. He looks upon them with delight, as the father on his children, as the bridegroom on his spouse, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Isa. lxii. 5</reference>. While those that depend on arms and armies, on chariots and horses, perish in the disappointment of their expectations, God's people, under his protection, are safe, for he shall deliver their soul from death when there seems to be but a step between them and it. If he do not deliver the body from temporal death, yet he will deliver the soul from spiritual and eternal death. Their souls, whatever happens, shall live and praise him, either in this world or in a better. From his bounty they shall be supplied with all necessaries. He shall <hi type="italic">keep them alive in famine;</hi> when others die for want, they shall live, which shall make it a distinguishing mercy. When visible means fail, God will find out some way or other to supply them. He does not say that he will give them abundance (they have no reason either to desire it or to expect it), but he will keep them alive; they shall not starve; and, when destroying judgments are abroad, it ought to be reckoned a great favour, for it is a very striking one, and lays us under peculiar obligations, to have our lives given us for a prey. Those that have the Lord for their God shall find him their help and their shield, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.20">v. 20</reference>. In their difficulties he will assist them; they shall be helped over them, helped through them. In their dangers he will secure them; they shall be helped over them, helped through them. In their dangers he will secure them, so that they shall not receive any real damage. (2.) The regard which God's people have to him and which we ought to have in consideration of this. [1.] We must wait for God. We must attend the motions of his providence, and accommodate ourselves to them, and patiently accommodate ourselves to them, and patiently expect the issue of them. Our souls must wait for him, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.20">v. 20</reference>. We must not only in word and tongue profess a believing regard to God, but it must be inward and sincere, a secret and silent attendance on him. [2.] We must rely on God, <hi type="italic">hope in his mercy,</hi> in the goodness of his nature, though we have not an express promise to depend upon. Those that fear God and his wrath must hope in God and his mercy; for there is no flying from God, but by flying to him. These pious dispositions will not only consist together, but befriend each other, a holy fear of God and yet at the same time a hope in his mercy. This is <hi type="italic">trusting in his holy name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.21">v. 21</reference>), in all that whereby he has made known himself to us, for our encouragement to serve him. [3.] We must rejoice in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.21">v. 21</reference>. Those do not truly rest in God, or do not know the unspeakable advantage they have by so doing, who do not rejoice in him at all times; because those that hope in God hope for an eternal fulness of joy in his presence. [4.] We must seek to him for that mercy which we hope in, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.22">v. 22</reference>. Our expectations from God are not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage, our applications to him; he will be sought unto for that which he has promised, and therefore the psalm concludes with a short but comprehensive prayer, "<hi type="italic">Let thy mercy, O Lord! be upon us;</hi> let us always have the comfort and benefit of it, not according as we merit from thee, but <hi type="italic">according as we hope in thee,</hi> that is, according to the promise which thou hast in thy word given to us and according to the faith which thou hast by thy Spirit and grace wrought in us." If, in singing <reference osisRef="Ps.33.12-Ps.33.22">these verses</reference>, we put forth a dependence upon God, and let out our desires towards him, we make melody with our hearts to the Lord.  <chapter eID="Ps.33"/> <div eID="gen10953" type="x-p"/>

entries.4248c8112ca26e7637faf9d133e4b23eab056b41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5810"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 33</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.33.1-Ps.33.22">Psa 33:1-22</reference>. A call to lively and joyous praise to God for His glorious attributes and works, as displayed in creation, and His general and special providence, in view of which, the Psalmist, for all the pious, professes trust and joy and invokes God's mercy.</title> <div sID="gen8845" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5810"/>1-3. The sentiment falls in with <reference osisRef="Ps.32.11">Psa 32:11</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.15">1Co 14:15</reference>). The instruments (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.3">Psa 92:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9">144:9</reference>) do not exclude the voice. <div eID="gen8845" type="x-p"/>
entries.1bf591728170eb2482163f3452bf92b05eaa86f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5812"/><div sID="gen8848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5812"/>4-9. Reasons for praise: first, God's truth, faithfulness, and mercy, generally; then, His creative power which all must honor. <div eID="gen8848" type="x-p"/>
entries.07161cc1d6b7b15134f9258e869b956ac1bce3a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5815"/><div sID="gen8852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5815"/>10-11. In God's providence He thwarts men's purposes and executes His own.<div eID="gen8852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heathen--</hi>literally, "nations." <div eID="gen8853" type="x-p"/>
entries.649f475e0f6016b2570922196bc9b6c37ce8f76e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5816"/><div sID="gen8854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5816"/>12-19. The inference from the foregoing in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.12">Psa 33:12</reference> is illustrated by God's special providence, underlying which is His minute knowledge of all men. <div eID="gen8854" type="x-p"/>
entries.e006cce428867bb4b4bbcc12acde64576dffc186: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5822"/><div sID="gen8863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5822"/><hi type="bold">20-22. waiteth--</hi>in earnest expectation. <div eID="gen8863" type="x-p"/>

entries.1ee4b3f886baafedf1add494ac3e1dec7d7d45b0: <div eID="gen19611" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19612" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19613" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19613" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19612" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19614" type="x-p"/> The Lord is praised for his works of creation, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.1-Psa.33.9">Psa 33:1-9</reference>; and for the stability of his own counsels, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.10">Psa 33:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.11">Psa 33:11</reference>. The blessedness of the people who have the knowledge of the true God, his grace, and providence, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.12-Psa.33.15">Psa 33:12-15</reference>. The vanity of all earthly dependence, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.16">Psa 33:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.17">Psa 33:17</reference>. The happiness of them that fear God, and trust in his mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.33.18-Psa.33.22">Psa 33:18-22</reference>. <div eID="gen19614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19615" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title in the Hebrew and it was probably written on no particular occasion, but was intended as a hymn of praise in order to celebrate the power, wisdom, and mercy of God. Creation and providence are its principal subjects; and these lead the psalmist to glance at different parts of the ancient Jewish history. In eight of Kennicott's MSS., this Psalm is written as a part of the preceding. <div eID="gen19615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19617" type="x-p"/> Rejoice in the Lord - It is very likely that the last verse of the preceding Psalm was formerly the first verse of this. As this Psalm has no title, the verse was the more easily separated. In the preceding Psalm we have an account of the happiness of the justified man: in this, such are taught how to glorify God, and to praise him for the great things he had done for them. <div eID="gen19617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19618" type="x-p"/> Praise is comely for the upright - It is right they should give thanks to Him, who is the fountain whence they have received all the good they possess and thankfulness becomes the lips of the upright.
entries.6c26f8179ffa43ab7f8ede23da75c5ca25fafd0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19619" type="x-p"/> Praise the Lord with harp - כנור kinnor; probably something like our harp: but Calmet thinks it the ancient testudo, or lyre with three strings. <div eID="gen19619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19620" type="x-p"/> The psalter - נבל nebel. Our translation seems to make a third instrument in this place, by rendering עשור asor, an instrument of ten strings; whereas they should both be joined together, for נבל עשור nebel-asor signifies the nebal, or nabla, with ten strings, or holes. Calmet supposes this to have resembled our harp. In one of Kennicott's MSS., this Psalm begins with the second verse.
entries.c58a3464b8d24a97370f4d50492f5bd92aa9b3d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19621" type="x-p"/> Sing unto him a new song - Do not wear out the old forms: fresh mercies call for new songs of praise and gratitude. <div eID="gen19621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19622" type="x-p"/> Play skilfully with a loud noise - Let sense and sound accompany each other; let the style of the music be suited to the words. This skill is possessed by few singers. They can make a loud noise, but they cannot adapt sound to sense.
entries.81709edef20ddabbe88df5e3eed9c7ecf6a0912f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19623" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord is right - He is infinitely wise, and can make no mistakes; and all his works are done in truth. All the words, laws, promises, and threatenings of God are perfectly true and just. The dispensations of his providence and mercy are equally so. When he rewards or punishes, it is according to truth and justice.
entries.ab80ece844018111f99a9859dfec1562721638d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19624" type="x-p"/> He loveth righteousness - What he delights in himself, he loves to see in his followers. <div eID="gen19624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19625" type="x-p"/> The earth is full of the goodness of the Lord - To hear its worthless inhabitants complain, one would think that God dispensed evil, not good. To examine the operation of his hand, every thing is marked with mercy and there is no place where his goodness does not appear. The overflowing kindness of God fills the earth. Even the iniquities of men are rarely a bar to his goodness: he causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends his rain upon the just and the unjust.
entries.3f68dc06327255313b9571c56c19bbcbc2fa2f4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19626" type="x-p"/> By the word of the Lord were the heavens made - This is illustrated in the <reference osisRef="Psa.33.9">Psa 33:9</reference> verse: "He spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast." This evidently refers to the account of the creation, as it stands in the first chapter of Genesis.
entries.141f5fe0e37fe4ace7766597fffa6b055e120f92: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19627" type="x-p"/> He gathereth the waters of the sea together - He separated the water from the earth and, while the latter was collected into continents, islands, mountains, hills, and valleys, the former was collected into one place, and called seas; and by his all-controlling power and providence the waters have been retained in their place, so that they have not returned to drown the earth: and he has so adapted the solar and sonar influence exerted on the waters, that the tides are only raised to certain heights, so that they cannot overflow the shores, nor become dissipated in the atmospheric regions. In this one economy there is a whole circle of science. The quantity of matter in the sun, moon, and in the earth, are all adjusted to each other in this astonishing provision: the course of the moon, and the diurnal and annual revolutions of the earth, are all concerned here; and so concerned, that it requires some of the nicest of the Newtonian calculations to ascertain the laws by which the whole is affected.
entries.98ae9f85a08387308ec4d17fb0fcbbd95f9e927d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19628" type="x-p"/> Let all the earth fear the Lord - He who has thus bound, can unloose; he who has created, can destroy. He has promised life and prosperity only to the godly; let the ungodly stand in awe of him.
entries.4e1bffb9df5373b6fa02e37417b40df79762d0a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19629" type="x-p"/> The counsel of the heathen to naught - This appears to be similar to what is mentioned in the second Psalm; the useless attempts of the Gentiles to prevent the extension of the kingdom of Christ in the earth: and it may refer to similar attempts of ungodly nations or men to prevent the promulgation of the Gospel, and the universal dissemination of truth in the world.
entries.b130c617f4f05d2dc071886e8f31b851fb4268b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19630" type="x-p"/> The counsel of the Lord - What he has determined shall be done. He determined to make a world, and he made it; to create man, and he created him. He determined that at a certain period God should be manifested in the flesh, and it was so; that he should taste death for every man, and he did so; that his Gospel should be preached in all the world; and behold it has already nearly overrun the whole earth. All his other counsels and thoughts, which refer to the future, shall be accomplished in their times.
entries.e8fd92d293595af9623352e8d2b8cfbb900d8f96: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19631" type="x-p"/> Blessed is the nation - O how happy is that nation which has יהוה Jehovah for its אלהים Elohim; the self-existent and eternal Lord for its covenant God; one who should unite himself to it by connections and ties the most powerful and endearing! The word אלהים Elohim, which we translate God, refers to that economy in which God is manifested in the flesh. <div eID="gen19631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19632" type="x-p"/> The people whom he hath chosen - The Jews, who were elected to be his heritage, whom he preserved as such for two thousand years, and whom he has reprobated because of their unbelief and rebellion, and elected the Gentiles in their place.
entries.8d3bd6c1f129258a3102fe52cfd49401c95e5b39: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19633" type="x-p"/> The Lord looketh from heaven - This and the following verse seem to refer to God's providence. He sees all that is done in the earth, and his eye is on all the children of men.
entries.86cde60433ff38414ec1f4c4f989b2c278af027c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19634" type="x-p"/> He fashioneth their hearts alike - He forms their hearts in unity; he has formed them alike; they are all the works of his hands: and he has formed them with the same powers, faculties, passions, etc.; body and spirit having the same essential properties in every human being.
entries.242f823e6adeec037f9f4d3fbaebf31798cec779: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19635" type="x-p"/> There is no king saved by the multitude of a host - Even in the midst of the most powerful and numerous army, no king is in safety unless he have God's protection. A king is but a man, and may as easily lose his life as one of his common soldiers. <div eID="gen19635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19636" type="x-p"/> A mighty man is not delivered by much strength - There are times in which his might can be of no avail to him: and unless the mighty, the wise, the honorable, etc., have the protection of God, there is no time in which their might may not be turned into weakness, their wisdom into folly, and their dignity into disgrace.
entries.264b7137bcafdc7897a87995534c01f13e1d1796: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19637" type="x-p"/> A horse is a vain thing for safety - Even the horse, with all his fleetness, is no sure means of escape from danger: the lion or the tiger can overtake him or he may stumble, fall, and destroy his rider.
entries.62490b4ce889bc9da6e4c6775144001b32ba368a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19638" type="x-p"/> Behold, the eye of the Lord - Though all the above are unavailing, yet here is one thing that can never fail; "the eye of the Lord" - the watchful providence of the Most High, "is upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy."
entries.5b70db090cd2f23544951974c490fdefdb0ca533: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19639" type="x-p"/> To deliver their soul from death - To watch over and protect them in all sudden dangers and emergencies, so that they shall not lose their Lives by any accident. <div eID="gen19639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19640" type="x-p"/> And to keep them alive in famine - Not only prevent sudden death by an instantaneous interposition of my power, but keep them from a lingering death, by extraordinary supplies granted them in an extraordinary manner; because I am all in all, and all everywhere.
entries.e26b5b02b0fc763bf4ca41f0b1c7c8cdfbfafaea: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19641" type="x-p"/> Our soul waiteth - Our whole life is employed in this blessed work; we trust in nothing but him; neither in multitudes of armed men, nor in natural strength, nor in the fleetest animals, nor in any thing human: we trust in Him alone "who is our help and our shield."
entries.b44996ffe6f5a1d90734de1c239b4a3aded90c52: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19642" type="x-p"/> For our heart shall rejoice in him - Here is the fruit of our confidence: our souls are always happy, because we have taken God for our portion.
entries.c6a106739a8c3ed07687fef0e2b3863a8129d70d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19643" type="x-p"/> Let thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us - We cannot abide in this state unless upheld by thee; and, as we disclaim all merit, we seek for a continuance of thy mercy, and this we cannot expect but in a continual dependence on thee. "Let thy mercy, O Lord be upon us, according as we hope in thee."  <chapter eID="Ps.33"/> <div eID="gen19643" type="x-p"/>

entries.5b71da9de869fe2cfd84cc6f8ab06e391d90c7f2: <div eID="gen9373" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Praise of the Ruler of the World as Being the Defender of His People</title> <div sID="gen9374" type="x-p"/> The Davidic Maskîl, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference>, is followed by an anonymous congregational song of a hymnic character, which begins just like the former closes. It owes its composition apparently to some deliverance of the nation from heathen oppression, which had resulted from God’s interposition and without war. Moreover it exhibits no trace of dependence upon earlier models, such as might compel us to assign a late date to it; the time of Jeremiah, for instance, which Hitzig adopts. The structure is symmetrical. Between the two hexastichs, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.1">Psa 33:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.20">Psa 33:20</reference>, the <hi type="italic">materia laudis</hi> is set forth in eight tetrastichs.
entries.a90ed666646dac8c1b8b5386c82c7d7be67e0f69: <reference osisRef="Ps.33.1-Ps.33.3">Psa 33:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9375" type="x-p"/> The call contained in this hexastich is addressed to the righteous and upright, who earnestly seek to live a godly and God-pleasing life, and the sole determining rule of whose conduct is the will and good pleasure of God. These alone know God, whose true nature finds in them a clear mirror; so on their part they are joyfully to confess what they possess in Him. For it is their duty, and at the same time their honour, to praise him, and make their boast in Him. נאוה is the feminine of the adjective נאוה (formed out of נאוי), as in <reference osisRef="Ps.147.1">Psa 147:1</reference>, cf. Pro 19:10. On כּנּור (lxx κιθάρα, κινύρα) and נבל (lxx ψαλτήριον, νάβλα, ναῦλα, etc.) vid., Introduction §II. נבל is the name given to the harp or lyre on account of its resemblance to a skin bottle or flash (root נב, to swell, to be distended), and נבל עשׂור, “harp of the decade,”' is the ten-stringed harp, which is also called absolutely עשׂור, and distinguished from the customary נבל, in Psa 92:4. By a comparison of the asyndeton expressions in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jer 11:19</reference>, Aben-Ezra understands by נבל עשור two instruments, contrary to the tenour of the words. Gecatilia, whom he controverts, is only so far in error as that he refers the ten to holes (נקבים) instead of to strings. The בּ is <hi type="italic">Beth instrum</hi>., just like the expression κιθαρίζειν ἐν κιθάραις, Rev 14:2. A “new song” is one which, in consequence of some new mighty deeds of God, comes from a new impulse of gratitude in the heart, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>, and frequently in the Psalms, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.10">Isa 42:10</reference>, Judith 6:13, Rev 5:9. In היטיבוּ the notions of <hi type="italic">scite</hi> and <hi type="italic">strenue, suaviter</hi> and <hi type="italic">naviter</hi>, blend. With בּתרוּעה, referring back to רננו, the call to praise forms, as it were, a circle as it closes.
entries.a226f06808626bdafe9fa7c898584f7b4ced3d0f: <reference osisRef="Ps.33.4-Ps.33.5">Psa 33:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen9375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9376" type="x-p"/> Now beings the body of the song. The summons to praise God is supported (1) by a setting forth of His praiseworthiness<note placement="foot">We have adopted the word “praiseworthiness” for the sake of conciseness of expression, in order to avoid an awkward periphrasis, in the sense of being worthy to be praised. - Tr.</note> (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) as the God of revelation in the kingdom of Grace. His word is ישׂר, upright in intention, and, without becoming in any way whatever untrue to itself, straightway fulfilling itself. His every act is an act in אמוּנה, truth, which verifies the truth of His word, and one which accomplishes itself. On אהב, equivalent to אהב הוּא, vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>; Psa 22:29. צדקה is righteousness as conduct; משׁפּט is right as a rule of judgment and a state or condition. חסד is an accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.64">Psa 119:64</reference> : <hi type="italic">misericordia Domini plena est terra</hi> (the introit for Misercordias Sunday or the second Sunday after Easter).
entries.aac33cc872dfa0d6965f2ce9c4e34c4100b3a1d1: <reference osisRef="Ps.33.6-Ps.33.9">Psa 33:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen9376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9377" type="x-p"/> God’s praiseworthiness (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) as the Creator of the world in the kingdom of Nature. Jahve’s דּבר is His almighty “Let there be;” and רוח פּיו (inasmuch as the breath is here regarded as the material of which the word is formed and the bearer of the word) is the command, or in general, the operation of His commanding omnipotence (<reference osisRef="Job.15.30">Job 15:30</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.4.9">Job 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Isa 34:16</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>). The heavens above and the waters beneath stand side by side as miracles of creation. The display of His power in the waters of the sea consists in His having confined them within fixed bounds and keeping them within these. נד is a pile, i.e., a piled up heap (Arabic <hi type="italic">nadd</hi>), and more especially an inference to harvest: like such a heap do the convex waters of the sea, being firmly held together, rise above the level of the continents. The expression is like that in <reference osisRef="Josh.3.13">Jos 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.3.15">Jos 3:15</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.15.8">Exo 15:8</reference>; although there the reference is to a miracle occurring in the course of history, and in this passage to a miracle of creation. כּנס refers to the heap itself, not to the walls of the storehouses as holding together. This latter figure is not introduced until <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.33.7">Psa 33:7</reference></hi>: the bed of the sea and those of the rivers are, as it were, אוצרות, treasuries or storehouses, in which God has deposited the deep, foaming waves or surging mass of waters. The inhabitants (ישׁבי, not יושׁבי) of the earth have cause to fear God who is thus omnipotent (מן, in the sense of falling back <hi type="italic">from</hi> in terror); for He need only speak the word and that which He wills comes into being out of nothing, as we see from the hexaëmeron or history of Creation, but which is also confirmed in human history (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.37">Lam 3:37</reference>). He need only command and it stands forth like an obedient servant, that appears in all haste at the call of his lord, Psa 119:91.
entries.d0142a82defe7e100ce9b7a4a54c3d44ebdd9aa5: <reference osisRef="Ps.33.10-Ps.33.11">Psa 33:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen9377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9378" type="x-p"/> His praiseworthiness (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) as the irresistible Ruler in the history of men. Since in <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.34">2Sa 15:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.14">2Sa 17:14</reference>, and frequently, הפר עצה is a common phrase, therefore heepiyr as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.34">Psa 89:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.19">Eze 17:19</reference>, is equivalent to הפר (Ges. §67, rem. 9). The perfects are not used in the abstract, but of that which has been experienced most recently, since the “new song” presupposes new matter. With <reference osisRef="Ps.33.11">Psa 33:11</reference> compare Pro 19:21. The עצת of God is the unity of the “thoughts of His heart,” i.e., of the ideas, which form the inmost part, the ultimate motives of everything that takes place. The whole history of the world is the uninterrupted carrying out of a divine plan of salvation, the primary object of which is His people, but in and with these are included humanity at large.
entries.43d801c8647ef408d0aaac65df28a845036ac992: <reference osisRef="Ps.33.12-Ps.33.19">Psa 33:12-19</reference> <div eID="gen9378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9379" type="x-p"/> Hence the call to praise God is supported (2) by a setting forth of that which His people possess in Him. This portion of the song is like a paraphrase of the אשׁרי in Deu 33:29. The theme in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.12">Psa 33:12</reference> is proved in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.13">Psa 33:13</reference> by the fact, that Jahve is the omniscient Ruler, because He is the Creator of men, without whose knowledge nothing is undertaken either secretly or openly, and especially if against His people.  Then in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.16">Psa 33:16</reference> it is supported by the fact, that His people have in Jahve a stronger defence than the greatest worldly power would be. Jahve is called the fashioner of all the hearts of men, as in Zec 12:1, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.12">Pro 24:12</reference>, as being their Maker. As such He is also the observer of all the works of men; for His is acquainted with their origin in the laboratory of the heart, which He as Creator has formed. Hupfeld takes יחד as an equalisation (<hi type="italic">pariter ac</hi>) of the two appositions; but then it ought to be וּמבין (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.49.3">Psa 49:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">Psa 49:11</reference>). The lxx correctly renders it καταμόνας, <hi type="italic">singillatim</hi>. It is also needless to translate it, as Hupfeld does: He who formed, <hi type="italic">qui finxit</hi>; for the hearts of men were not from the very first created all at one time, but the primeval impartation of spirit-life is continued at every birth in some mysterious way. God is the Father of spirits, Heb 12:9. For this very reason everything that exists, even to the most hidden thing, is encompassed by His omniscience and omnipotence. He exercises an omniscient control over all things, and makes all things subservient to the designs of His plan of the universe, which, so far as His people are concerned, is the plan of salvation. Without Him nothing comes to pass; but through Him everything takes place. The victory of the king, and the safety of the warrior, are not their own works. Their great military power and bodily strength can accomplish nothing without God, who can also be mighty in the feeble.  Even for purposes of victory (תּשׁוּעה, cf. ישׁוּעה, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.2">Psa 21:2</reference>) the war-horse is שׁקר, i.e., a thing that promises much, but can in reality do nothing; it is not its great strength, by which it enables the trooper to escape (ימלּט). “The horse,” says Solomon in <reference osisRef="Prov.21.31">Pro 21:31</reference>, “is equipped for the day of battle, but התּשׁוּעה לה, Jahve’s is the victory,” He giveth it to whomsoever He will. The ultimate ends of all things that come to pass are in His hands, and - as Psa 33:18. say, directing special attention to this important truth by הנּה - the eye of this God, that is to say the final aim of His government of the world, is directed towards them that fear Him, is pointed at them that hope in His mercy (למיחלים). In <reference osisRef="Ps.33.19">Psa 33:19</reference>, the object, לחסדּו, is expanded by way of example. From His mercy or loving-kindness, not from any acts of their own, conscious of their limited condition and feebleness, they look for protection in the midst of the greatest peril, and for the preservation of their life in famine. <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference> is very similar; but the one passage sounds as independent as the other.
entries.9e41a5f2cf0b2d68cfffbf30a0010bd96c0d8f55: <reference osisRef="Ps.33.20-Ps.33.22">Psa 33:20-22</reference> <div eID="gen9379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9380" type="x-p"/> Accordingly, in this closing hexastich, the church acknowledges Him as its help, its shield, and its source of joy. Besides the passage before us, חכּה occurs in only one other instance in the Psalter, viz., Psa 106:13. This word, which belongs to the group of words signifying hoping and waiting, is perhaps from the root חך (Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥk'</hi>, <hi type="italic">ḥkâ</hi>, <hi type="italic">firmiter constringere sc. nodum</hi>), to be firm, compact, like קוּה from קוה, to pull tight or fast, cf. the German <hi type="italic">harren</hi> (to wait) and <hi type="italic">hart</hi> (hard, compact). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.33.20">Psa 33:20</reference></hi> we still hear the echo of the primary passage <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deu 33:29</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.33.26">Deu 33:26</reference>). The emphasis, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11">Psa 115:9-11</reference>, rests upon הוּא, into which בּו, in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.21">Psa 33:21</reference>, puts this thought, viz., He is the unlimited sphere, the inexhaustible matter, the perennial spring of our joy. The second כּי confirms this subjectively. His holy Name is His church’s ground of faith, of love, and of hope; for from thence comes its salvation. It can boldly pray that the mercy of the Lord may be upon it, for it waits upon Him, and man’s waiting or hoping and God’s giving are reciprocally conditioned. This is the meaning of the כּאשׁר. God is true to His word. The <hi type="italic">Te Deum laudamus</hi> of Ambrose closes in the same way.  <chapter eID="Ps.33"/> <div eID="gen9380" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 33.
David, or whoever was the author of this psalm, in order to excite believers to praise God, founds his argument upon the general providence of God, by which he sustains, protects, and governs the whole world. Afterwards he celebrates God’s paternal kindness towards his chosen people, showing at the same time how necessary it is that the godly should be cherished by his special care.
Psalm 33:1-4
1. Rejoice in Jehovah, ye righteous; praise is comely
“Ou, digne d’estre aimee par les,” etc. — Fr. marg. “Or, is worthy of being loved by them.”
for the upright. 2. Praise Jehovah upon the harp; sing unto him upon the viol, and an instrument of ten strings. 3. Sing a new song to him; sing loudly with joyfulness: 4. For the word of Jehovah is right; and all his works are in faithfulness.
“Fideles, c’est, fermes et permanentes.” — Fr. marg. “Faithful, that is, firm and permanent.”
 
1. Rejoice in Jehovah, ye righteous. Here the inspired writer addresses believers or the righteous by name, because they alone are capable of proclaiming the glory of God. Unbelievers, who have never tasted his goodness, cannot praise him from the heart, and God has no pleasure in his name being pronounced by their unholy tongues. But the context shows more distinctly why this exhortation is suitable for believers only. Many, accordingly, expound the latter clause, Praise is comely for the upright, as meaning, that if the ungodly or hypocrites attempt this exercise, it will turn to the reproach and dishonor of God rather than to his praise; nay, more, that they only profane his holy name. It is, no doubt, very true, as I have already remarked, that God creates for himself a church in the world by gracious adoption, for the express purpose, that his name may be duly praised by witnesses suitable for such a work. But the real meaning of the clause, Praise is comely for the upright, is, that there is no exercise in which they can be better employed. And, assuredly, since God by his daily benefits furnishes them with such matter for celebrating his glory, and since his boundless goodness, as we have elsewhere seen, is laid up as a peculiar treasure for them, it were disgraceful and utterly unreasonable for them to be silent in the praises of God. The amount of the matter is, that the principal exercise in which it becomes the righteous to be employed is to publish among men the righteousness, goodness, and power of God, the knowledge of which is implanted in their minds. Following other interpreters, I have translated the clause, Praise is comely, but the word rendered comely may also be properly rendered desirable, if we view it as derived from the Hebrew word אוה, avah, which signifies to wish or desire. And certainly, when God allures believers so sweetly, it is proper that they employ themselves in celebrating his praises with their whole hearts. It is also to be observed, that when the prophet, after having in the first clause used the appellation, the righteous, immediately adds the words, the upright, which comprehend the inward integrity of the heart, he defines what true righteousness is, or in what it consists.
